titre: Raleigh, 1603: the accuser he was never shown
accroche: Winchester, November 17, 1603: Walter Raleigh is tried on the statement of an absent man and demands to see him. In 2004, the U.S. Supreme Court remembers.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 17, 1603, in the great hall of Winchester Castle, Walter Raleigh is tried for treason. He is accused of taking part in the Main Plot, a conspiracy against King James I. He conducts his own defense. The prosecution's main piece of evidence is the signed statement of a friend, Henry Brooke, Lord Cobham, who implicated him in an interrogation before the Privy Council and then in a letter. Both texts are read to the jury. Cobham himself is not in the room.

## What Raleigh asks for

Raleigh does not deny that a man wrote what is being read. He disputes what it is worth. Cobham, he says in essence, is entirely at the king's mercy: excusing himself would do him no good, but by accusing someone else he can hope for a favor. So he demands, according to the accounts of the trial: “Call my accuser before my face.” He says he is being tried as if by the Spanish Inquisition.

The judges refuse. Cobham will not come and will not be questioned. The jury finds Raleigh guilty and he is sentenced to death. James I ultimately spares his life. He remains in the Tower of London until 1616, where he writes a *History of the World* that he will never finish. One of his judges would later acknowledge that English justice had never been so degraded as by this conviction.

## Four centuries later

On March 8, 2004, the U.S. Supreme Court hands down *Crawford v. Washington*, in an opinion by Justice Scalia. The case has nothing to do with a conspiracy: in the State of Washington, a recorded statement made to the police by an accused man's wife was presented to the jury without the defense having been able to question her. The Court holds that this violates the accused's right, guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, to be confronted with the witnesses against him. To ground its reading of that right, it recalls the scene at Winchester. It holds that a statement made to serve as testimony, by someone who does not appear in court, is admissible only if its author is unavailable at trial and the accused has previously had an opportunity to cross-examine him. That is the rule laid down by this 2004 ruling, in American law.

## The shift

A statement read in the absence of its author cannot be tested. Raleigh suspects Cobham of accusing in order to save himself, and he cannot ask him: that Cobham wrote this text is not in doubt, but what he stood to gain by writing it is something to be asked out loud, in front of the accused. A trial that has only paper to work with judges texts, not witnesses. It remains to be asked how many convictions since have rested on papers that no accused was able to question.

repere.texte: On March 8, 2004, in Crawford v. Washington, the U.S. Supreme Court (opinion of Justice Scalia) cites Walter Raleigh's 1603 trial, where the accused demanded his accuser in vain, and holds that a statement made to serve as testimony by an absent person is admissible only if its author is unavailable and the accused has previously had an opportunity to cross-examine him.
repere.source: Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Justice Scalia

carte.punch: In 1603, Raleigh demands his accuser. The court refuses, and the jury convicts him.
carte.idee: Walter Raleigh is convicted at Winchester in 1603 on the statement of an absent man, Lord Cobham, who had a reason to accuse him. Four centuries later, the U.S. Supreme Court cites that scene to read the right to confront one's accusers.
carte.source_courte: Crawford v. Washington, U.S. Supreme Court, 2004

quiz.question: What objection does Raleigh raise to Cobham's statement being read to the jury in Cobham's absence?
choix: The self-interest of an accuser hoping for a favor from the king cannot be tested unless he stands before the accused
It was written by a court clerk and not by Cobham himself
It was not read in full to the jury before it deliberated on the verdict
It comes from a foreigner, whereas only a subject of the king may testify against another
quiz.explication: Raleigh does not dispute the existence of the text but its worth: Cobham, at the king's mercy, can hope for a favor by accusing, and only a face-to-face confrontation allows him to be asked about it. The other three answers invent material defects (author, partial reading, nationality) that have nothing to do with his argument, and the statement was indeed read to the jury.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the main piece of evidence behind the accusation against Raleigh in 1603?
choix: The oral testimony of two soldiers present when the plot was being prepared
The signed statement of Lord Cobham, read to the jury without his being present
A letter from James I expressly ordering Raleigh's conviction
Raleigh's own written confession, obtained before the trial
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The prosecution relies on Lord Cobham's signed statement, made before the Privy Council and then in a letter, and read to the jury while Cobham is not in the room.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of Walter Raleigh after his death sentence in 1603?
choix: He is executed a few weeks later at the Tower of London
He is pardoned immediately and leaves England for the colonies
He escapes from the Tower of London before being recaptured and executed
James I spares his life; he remains in the Tower of London until 1616
quiz_supplementaire.explication: James I spares Raleigh's life after his death sentence; he remains a prisoner in the Tower of London until 1616, where he writes a History of the World that he will never finish.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What facts lie behind the 2004 ruling in Crawford v. Washington?
choix: A recorded statement by an accused man's wife, presented to the jury without cross-examination
A video recording of a suspect's interrogation broadcast without his consent
An anonymous witness's refusal to appear before a federal court
A disputed ballistics report, with no access to the police laboratory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the State of Washington, the recorded statement of an accused man's wife is presented to the jury without the defense having been able to cross-examine her, which leads to the 2004 ruling.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What rule does the Supreme Court lay down in Crawford v. Washington for admitting an absent person's statement?
choix: It is admissible if a judge finds it credible in light of the file
It is admissible only if its author is unavailable and the accused was able to cross-examine him beforehand
It is admissible if two independent witnesses corroborate it in writing
It is never admissible, whatever the circumstances
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court holds that a testimonial statement by an absent person is admissible only if its author is unavailable at trial and the accused has previously had an opportunity to cross-examine him.
